items.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a real-world probability measure P from a risk-neutral probability measure Q in this lesson?

options.label: P describes modeled real-world frequencies; Q supplies no-arbitrage pricing weights
P and Q must assign the same probability to every event
Q assigns certainty to every traded payoff

items.explanation: P and Q can weight the same outcomes differently. P is the modeled real-world measure; Q is selected so discounted traded prices satisfy the model's no-arbitrage pricing condition.

items.prompt: An analyst says, 'After changing from P to Q, uncertainty disappears and volatility is absorbed by the measure.' Which response is correct for the standard diffusion result taught here?

options.label: The change reweights outcomes and changes drift, but it does not remove randomness or the diffusion volatility
The change makes every future payoff deterministic
The change sets every volatility parameter to zero

items.explanation: Risk-neutral valuation changes the probability weights used for pricing. In the standard change-of-measure result, the drift changes while the diffusion coefficient remains; uncertainty is still present.

items.prompt: At T, a signed payoff is USD 120 with Q-probability 0.70 and USD 20 with Q-probability 0.30. The deterministic discount factor is D(0,T) = 0.96. What is its time-zero risk-neutral value in USD?
items.explanation: First compute the Q-expectation: 0.70 × 120 + 0.30 × 20 = 90 future USD. Then discount: 0.96 × 90 = USD 86.40 at time zero.

items.prompt: A contract has signed terminal payoffs of USD 200, USD 50, and USD -40 in three disjoint exhaustive scenarios. Their Q-probabilities are 0.20, 0.50, and 0.30, and D(0,T) = 0.94. What is the time-zero risk-neutral value in USD?
items.explanation: The Q-expected terminal payoff is 0.20 × 200 + 0.50 × 50 + 0.30 × (-40) = USD 53. Discounting gives 0.94 × 53 = USD 49.82.
